title: Bit prefixes and bitboards
sub: Maximum XOR greedily from the top bit, queries with a limit (#1707), bitboards, autotiles and fog of war
cards/0/title: Maximum XOR: the problem and the cost of brute force
cards/0/body:
Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array (LeetCode #421): find the maximum of nums[i] ^ nums[j]; n ≤ 2·10⁵, 0 ≤ nums[i] < 2³¹. Example: [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8] → 28 = 5 ^ 25.

Trying all pairs is n²/2 = 2·10¹⁰ operations at n = 2·10⁵: minutes instead of a second. Sorting does not help: XOR is not monotonic, and large numbers do not give a large XOR — 25 ^ 10 = 19, while 25 ^ 5 = 28.

The signal is “maximise a XOR”. Bit k is worth 2ᵏ, and all the lower bits together are worth 2ᵏ − 1, which is less. So the answer’s bits are decided greedily from the top: if bit k can be a 1, take it — no combination of lower bits can outweigh it.
cards/1/q: Bit 4 of the answer can be a 1, but only with a partner that leaves zeros in bits 3..0. Another partner gives 0 in bit 4 and 1s in all of bits 3..0. Which do you choose?
cards/1/options/0: The 1 in bit 4: 10000₂ = 16 is more than 01111₂ = 15
cards/1/options/1: The 1s in bits 3..0: there are four of them against one
cards/1/options/2: You have to explore both branches to the end and compare
cards/1/explain: Bit 4 is worth 16, and all the lower bits together 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. A 1 in the higher bit beats any combination of lower ones, so the greedy choice from the top bit is never wrong and there is no need to explore branches.
cards/1/wrong/1: You compare values, not the number of 1s: 01111₂ = 15 < 10000₂ = 16.
cards/1/wrong/2: Exploring branches means 2³¹ options. It is unnecessary: the higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together.
cards/2/body:
Build the answer from the top down. Say the higher bits of the answer are already known — that is best. We want a 1 in the next bit k: the candidate is cand = (best << 1) | 1. It is reachable if there are two numbers whose prefixes — the higher bits, v >> k — XOR to cand.

The check in O(n): put all the prefixes into a HashSet and, for each p, ask whether p ^ cand is there. This is Two Sum with the sum replaced by XOR: p ^ q = cand ⇔ q = p ^ cand — XOR is its own inverse. Found it — bit k of the answer is 1, otherwise 0, and on to the next bit.

31 bits × n numbers is O(31·n) ≈ 6·10⁶ operations, with O(n) memory. Instead of 31 sets you can build a binary trie once, bit by bit from the top: each number is a path of 31 steps, and for x you follow the opposite bits wherever possible. Also O(31·n); tries are covered in depth in the data structure design unit.
cards/3/q: On [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8] this code returns 25 instead of 28. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/3/explain: The code asks whether some number has the prefix cand, but the question is whether a pair of prefixes XORs to cand. So it simply follows the bits of the largest number and finds 25. The fix: foreach (int p in prefixes) — prefixes.Contains(p ^ cand).
cards/4/title: A limit m: Maximum XOR With an Element (#1707)
cards/4/body:
Maximum XOR With an Element From Array (#1707, Hard): queries [x, m] ask for the maximum of x ^ nums[j] over nums[j] ≤ m, or −1 if there are no such numbers; n and the number of queries go up to 10⁵. #421 is the same question without the limit m.

Offline means answering the queries in whatever order suits you. Sort nums, sort the queries by m, and before each query add every number ≤ m. The set only grows; nothing ever needs removing. The answers are put back at the queries’ original indices.

Walking down the bits. For x go from the top bit: you want y to have the bit opposite to x’s, which makes a 1 in x ^ y. If one of the added numbers continues the chosen path with that bit, go there and set the answer’s bit. If not, go with the same bit, and the answer’s bit is 0. The prefixes are stored by level: levels[k] holds every v >> k; this is a trie stored level by level.

In the trace y’s path is written in bits from the top: “prefix 00” means the number has zeros in the two highest bits of the trace. The trace starts at the highest bit present in the input; everything above is zero.
cards/5/task: Step through the trace on nums = [5, 2, 4, 6, 6, 3] with the queries x:m = 12:4, 8:1, 6:3. The queries go in order of growing m, and the set of numbers grows. The rig asks twice what the code does next.
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: y goes on with 1: no prefix 000, bit 1 of the answer is 0
cards/5/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: y goes on with 0: bit 1 of the answer is 1
cards/5/goal/asks/0/q: Query 6:3, the set holds 2 and 3 (0010₂ and 0011₂). Bits 3 and 2 are decided, y’s path is 00. Bit 1: x = 0110₂ has a 1 here. What next?
cards/5/goal/asks/0/explain: We want y to have a 0 here — the path 000. But both numbers have bit 1 set (001·), so nobody continues the path 000. We are forced along 001, and bit 1 of x ^ y is 0. The greedy choice does not suffer: bit 2 is already taken, and it is worth more than all the lower bits together.
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: y goes on with 0: 2 and 3 have the prefix 00, bit 2 of the answer is 1
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: y goes on with 1 — towards the 4: it is the largest allowed number
cards/5/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: y goes on with 1: there is no prefix 00
cards/5/goal/asks/1/q: Query 12:4: the 4 was just added, the set holds 2, 3 and 4 (0010₂, 0011₂, 0100₂). Bit 3 is taken, y’s path is 0. Bit 2: x = 1100₂ has a 1 here. What next?
cards/5/goal/asks/1/explain: We want y to have a 0 in bit 2 — then x ^ y gets a 1 here. The 2 and the 3 have the prefix 00, so we take it. The 4 (01··) drops out, even though it was just added and is the largest: with it bit 2 of x ^ y is 0, and 12 ^ 4 = 8. The walk goes on to y = 3 and the answer 12 ^ 3 = 15.
cards/6/body:
An 8×8 board — 64 cells — fits in one ulong: cell (x, y) is bit y * 8 + x. Such a bitboard answers a question about the whole board with one operation: occupied is white | black, empty is ~occupied, the number of pieces is a popcount, moving every piece one row up is << 8.

Moving right in x is << 1, but a piece on the right edge jumps to the left edge of the next row. That is why horizontal shifts are masked: (b << 1) & ~FileA, where FileA is the bits of column x = 0. Iterating over pieces is Kernighan’s trick from the first lesson: the cell of the lowest piece is the number of trailing zeros (BitOperations.TrailingZeroCount, in Unity math.tzcnt), and b &= b − 1 removes it. A ulong has no unary minus, so the lowest piece as a mask is written b & (~b + 1).

Chess engines are built this way, and in games so are tic-tac-toe (9 bits and 8 winning masks: (board & line) == line), connect four, and the Game of Life on a small board in a few shifts.
cards/7/q: An 8×8 bitboard: cell (x, y) is bit y * 8 + x. The only piece is on (7, 2). Where does it end up after b << 1 without a mask?
cards/7/options/0: On (0, 3): bit 23 → bit 24, the start of the next row
cards/7/options/1: It disappears: it went off the edge of the board
cards/7/options/2: On (7, 3): a shift one row up
cards/7/explain: (7, 2) is bit 2 · 8 + 7 = 23. Shifting by 1 gives bit 24 = 3 · 8 + 0, that is (0, 3): the piece jumped from the right edge to the left edge of the next row. That is why the right shift is masked: (b << 1) & ~FileA.
cards/7/wrong/1: Only bits pushed past bit 63 of the whole ulong are lost. Bit 24 is inside — the piece is simply in the wrong place.
cards/7/wrong/2: Moving one row up is << 8, not << 1.
cards/8/body:
Autotiling. A wall tile picks its sprite from its neighbours. Each neighbour gets a bit: north 1, east 2, south 4, west 8. The mask 0..15 is directly the index into a 16-sprite tileset: no branches, no table of conditions. With diagonals there are 8 bits and 256 masks, but a corner neighbour only affects the sprite if both edges next to it are filled — otherwise the corner is hidden anyway. After this rule there are 47 distinct masks left, hence the classic 47-tile tileset. In Unity the RuleTile from the 2D Tilemap Extras package does this, but in an interview you are asked to write the mask by hand.

Fog of war. A 64×64 map is 64 rows of one ulong each. What is visible right now is the mask visible: it is built by ORing the units’ vision circles — precomputed masks shifted to each unit’s position. What has been explored is explored[y] |= visible[y], and it never goes dark. 4,096 cells are 512 bytes per layer, an update is 64 operations instead of 4,096 checks, and the same masks feed the fog texture for the shader.
cards/8/deep:
Where 47 comes from. Four edges give 16 options. A corner counts only when both its edges are filled: with k pairs of adjacent filled edges you get 2ᵏ corner options. Among the 16 edge masks, 7 have no such pair, 4 have one, 4 have two (three edges), and 1 has four (all edges). 7 + 4·2 + 4·4 + 1·16 = 47. The indices 0..255 are squeezed into 0..46 by a 256-entry table computed once.

Fog wider than 64 cells. A row becomes an array of ulong, and shifting a vision mask to a unit’s position crosses word boundaries: some bits move into the neighbouring word (w[i] << s | w[i − 1] >> (64 − s), with s = 0 as a special case: a shift by 64 on a ulong shifts nothing). Rows are independent, so they are convenient to compute in an IJobParallelFor under Burst, where math.countbits and math.tzcnt on ulong become instructions.

Ready-made structures. .NET has BitArray (bits in an int[], with And, Or, Xor over the whole array). The com.unity.collections package has NativeBitArray and UnsafeBitArray for Jobs. But in an interview you are expected to lay the cells out in ulongs yourself and name the cost: 64 cells per operation.
cards/9/q: Autotile mask: north 1, east 2, south 4, west 8. A wall cell has wall neighbours above and to the left. What is the tile index?
cards/9/explain: Above is north, bit 1; left is west, bit 8. 1 | 8 = 9 = 1001₂. The index is the mask itself: no ifs over combinations of neighbours.
cards/9/wrong/1: 3 = 1 | 2 is north and east, that is above and to the right.
cards/9/wrong/3: 12 = 4 | 8 is south and west, below and to the left.
cards/10/q: You are solving Maximum XOR of Two Numbers out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: n up to 2·10⁵, the numbers are non-negative and below 2³¹
cards/10/items/1: Brute force: all pairs — O(n²), 2·10¹⁰ at n = 2·10⁵
cards/10/items/2: Idea: greedily from the top bit — bit k is worth more than all lower bits together
cards/10/items/3: Code: prefixes v >> k in a HashSet, is p ^ cand there
cards/10/items/6: Variations: a bitwise trie; with a limit m — offline by m (#1707)
cards/10/explain: First the constraints (they rule out brute force), then the greedy principle, and only then the way to test a bit — the set of prefixes. The trie and #1707 come last: in a senior interview a follow-up to the problem often comes right after.
cards/11/q: Match the condition to the technique.
cards/11/pairs/1/0: Is there a pair with p ^ q = cand
cards/11/pairs/1/1: HashSet and a lookup of p ^ cand
cards/11/pairs/4/1: Neighbour mask as the tile index
